title: Climate Calculations for Japan
text:
About the data
日本語はこちら（JP）
This documentation explains how to process climate variables using the Japan Meteorological Agency’s Mesh Climatology 2020.
The FAO-56 ET0 chapter adds a separate workflow for NARO daily inputs from 2008–2018, alongside the existing Thornthwaite PET workflow based on 1991–2020 JMA/MLIT monthly normals. Reference ET0 and temperature-based PET have different definitions, inputs and periods. The new chapter executes synthetic examples only; permission to share the NARO-derived ET0 and precipitation tables or maps remains unconfirmed.
This project uses the National Land Numerical Information (MLIT) Average Value Mesh Data.
This repository does not redistribute original or processed datasets. Please download required data on your own.
Please review the NLNI terms of use, especially the source attribution requirement.

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Load libraries

library(tools)
library(sf)

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Set the data directory

data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROJECT_DATA_DIR")
# If the environment variable is not set:
# data_dir <- "data"

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Extract ZIP files

zip_output_dir <- file.path("data", "climate_mesh_data")
dir.create(zip_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

zip_files <- list.files(
  file.path(data_dir, "climate_mesh_data_zip"),
  pattern = "^G02-22_.*\\.zip$",
  full.names = TRUE
)
file_names <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(zip_files))
lapply(zip_files, unzip, overwrite = TRUE, exdir = zip_output_dir)

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Read shapefiles

data_list <- list()
data_paths <- list.files(
  zip_output_dir,
  pattern = "^G02-22_.*\\.shp$",
  full.names = TRUE,
  recursive = TRUE
)

for (i in seq_along(data_paths)) {
  path <- data_paths[i]
  name <- file_path_sans_ext(basename(path))
  data_list[[name]] <- st_read(path)
}
sf_climate <- do.call(rbind, data_list)

df_label <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "manual/mesh_climate_data_labels.csv"),
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
names(sf_climate) <- make.names(c(df_label$name_en, "geometry"))

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Convert values
Values are scaled by 10 in the source data; divide by 10 to recover original units. Missing values are encoded as 999999.

col_index <- c(
  grep("precipitation", names(sf_climate)),
  grep("temperature", names(sf_climate)),
  grep("sunshine_duration", names(sf_climate)),
  grep("global_solar_radiation", names(sf_climate))
)
indices_snow <- grep("maximum_snow_depth", names(sf_climate))

NA_value <- 999999
df <- st_drop_geometry(sf_climate)
df[, col_index][df[, col_index] == NA_value] <- NA
df[, col_index] <- df[, col_index] * 0.1
df[, indices_snow][df[, indices_snow] == NA_value] <- 0
sf_climate <- st_set_geometry(df, st_geometry(sf_climate))

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Extract longitude and latitude

sf_climate$longitude <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(sf_climate))[, 1]
sf_climate$latitude <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(sf_climate))[, 2]

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Save data

save_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "climate_mesh_data_joined")
dir.create(save_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
saveRDS(sf_climate, file.path(save_dir, "climate_mesh_data.rds"))

title: Prepare Climate Data
text:
Save as CSV

df_climate <- st_drop_geometry(sf_climate)
write.csv(
  df_climate,
  file.path(save_dir, "climate_mesh_data.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

title: Calculate Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
text:
Load libraries
日本語はこちら（JP）
This chapter calculates potential evapotranspiration (PET) using the Thornthwaite method (Thornthwaite 1948) with the SPEI package (Beguería and Vicente-Serrano 2023).
library(sf)
library(SPEI)

title: Calculate Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
text:
Load data

data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROJECT_DATA_DIR")
# data_dir <- "data" # if PROJECT_DATA_DIR is not set
sf_climate <- readRDS(file.path(
  data_dir,
  "climate_mesh_data_joined/climate_mesh_data.rds"
))

title: Calculate Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
section: Create a data frame for PET calculation
text:
Create a data frame for PET calculation

latitudes <- sf_climate$latitude
df_temp <- sf_climate[, grep("mean_temperature", names(sf_climate))]
df_temp <- st_drop_geometry(df_temp)
df_temp <- df_temp[, 1:12]

keep <- complete.cases(df_temp)
removed_rows <- which(!keep)

df_temp_clean <- df_temp[keep, ]
sf_climate_clean <- sf_climate[keep, ]
row.names(df_temp_clean) <- sf_climate_clean$mesh_code_3rd

title: Calculate Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
Calculate Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
text:
Shape PET data

df_pet <- as.data.frame(pet_month)
names(df_pet) <- paste0("PET", 1:12)
df_pet$PET_year <- rowSums(df_pet)

title: Calculate Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
text:
Join PET to climate data

df_pet$mesh_code_3rd <- row.names(df_temp_clean)
sf_merged <- merge(
  sf_climate,
  df_pet,
  by = "mesh_code_3rd",
  all.x = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE
)
df_merged <- st_drop_geometry(sf_merged)

title: Calculate Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
text:
Save data

save_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "climate_mesh_data_joined")
saveRDS(sf_merged, file.path(save_dir, "climate_mesh_data_with_pet.rds"))
write.csv(
  df_merged,
  file.path(save_dir, "climate_mesh_data_with_pet.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

title: Calculate Aridity Index
text:
Load libraries
日本語はこちら（JP）
This chapter calculates the Aridity Index (AI). AI is a dryness indicator defined here as precipitation (\(P\)) divided by potential evapotranspiration (\(PET\)) (World Atlas of Desertification 1992). Lower values indicate drier conditions because potential evapotranspiration is larger relative to precipitation.
Several definitions of aridity index are used in the literature. In this chapter, the following equation is used:
\[AI = \frac{P}{PET}\]
where \(P\) is precipitation and \(PET\) is potential evapotranspiration.
library(sf)

title: Calculate Aridity Index
text:
Load data
In this repository, the PROJECT_DATA_DIR environment variable points to the directory where input and output data are stored. Change it as needed for your local environment.

data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROJECT_DATA_DIR")
sf_climate <- readRDS(file.path(
  data_dir,
  "climate_mesh_data_joined/climate_mesh_data_with_pet.rds"
))

title: Calculate Aridity Index
text:
Calculate Aridity Index
First, calculate the annual Aridity Index and add it to the sf_climate object as a new aridity_index column. When PET is zero, negative, or missing, the Aridity Index is undefined, so the value is set to NA.

sf_climate$aridity_index <- ifelse(
  is.na(sf_climate$PET_year) | sf_climate$PET_year <= 0,
  NA_real_,
  sf_climate$precipitation_year / sf_climate$PET_year
)

Then, calculate monthly Aridity Index values. The monthly columns are named from aridity_index_Jan to aridity_index_Dec.

month_labels <- month.abb
for (month in seq_along(month_labels)) {
  month_label <- month_labels[month]
  precipitation_col <- paste0("precipitation_", month_label)
  pet_col <- paste0("PET", month)
  aridity_index_col <- paste0("aridity_index_", month_label)
  pet_values <- sf_climate[[pet_col]]

  sf_climate[[aridity_index_col]] <- ifelse(
    is.na(pet_values) | pet_values <= 0,
    NA_real_,
    sf_climate[[precipitation_col]] / pet_values
  )
}

title: Calculate Aridity Index
text:
Save data
Save the result in both RDS and CSV formats. Change the output path as needed.

saveRDS(
  sf_climate,
  file.path(
    data_dir,
    "climate_mesh_data_joined/climate_mesh_data_with_aridity_index.rds"
  )
)
df_climate <- st_drop_geometry(sf_climate)
write.csv(
  df_climate,
  file.path(
    data_dir,
    "climate_mesh_data_joined/climate_mesh_data_with_aridity_index.csv"
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)

title: Calculate FAO-56 Reference Evapotranspiration (ET₀)
text:
Scope and relation to PET
日本語はこちら（JP）
This chapter uses the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith equation to calculate daily reference evapotranspiration (ET₀) and combine it into monthly and seasonal totals. FAO-56 refers to Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, the technical guide published by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
All examples run on this page use synthetic data or a published FAO example. The page does not include actual NARO data or maps made from them.
Neither quantity is measured forest evapotranspiration. Comparing these products mixes method, input and period differences; it does not isolate a method effect. The existing PET and AI chapters retain their original definitions and inputs. Precipitation is needed for AI, but is not an input to the ET0 equation.
source("R/et0_support.R")
source("R/pipeline_p0_et0.R")

WarningUsing NARO data



Before using the data, read NARO’s usage terms and application guide. Each user should apply for access and handle the data according to the terms. This site provides calculation code and synthetic examples, not NARO data.
Permission to share the ET₀ and precipitation tables prepared for this project, or maps made from them, has not been confirmed, so they are not published here. The code and documentation licenses do not grant permission to redistribute weather data. Keep original files unchanged and actual data outside Git.

title: Calculate FAO-56 Reference Evapotranspiration (ET₀)
text:
Daily equation and assumptions
The implementation uses FAO-56 equation 6:
ET0=0.408Δ(Rn−G)+γ900T+273u2(es−ea)Δ+γ(1+0.34u2).
ET_0 = \frac{0.408\Delta(R_n-G)
 + \gamma\frac{900}{T+273}u_2(e_s-e_a)}
 {\Delta+\gamma(1+0.34u_2)}.

ET0 is in mm/day; T is daily mean temperature (°C); Rn and G are net radiation and soil heat flux (MJ/m²/day); u2 is wind speed at 2 m (m/s); es and ea are saturation and actual vapour pressure (kPa); Delta and gamma are the slope of the saturation vapour-pressure curve and psychrometric constant (kPa/°C).

Daily soil heat flux G is zero; reference albedo is 0.23.
Saturation pressure is averaged from daily maximum and minimum temperature. Actual pressure uses mean relative humidity, rather than paired RH extremes.
Source wind is assumed to be at 10 m and converted to 2 m. The source measurement height remains unconfirmed.
Interior gaps of at most two days in RH and wind are linearly interpolated separately within each calendar year. Longer gaps and gaps at year edges remain missing. Other input variables are not interpolated.
Missing inputs propagate to daily ET0, monthly totals and multi-year means. Sums and means do not use na.rm = TRUE.
Negative computed ET0 is retained, without clipping to zero.

With e∘(T)=0.6108exp⁡[17.27T/(T+237.3)]e^\circ(T)=0.6108\exp[17.27T/(T+237.3)], mean-RH vapour pressure is ea=(RHmean/100)[e∘(Tmax)+e∘(Tmin)]/2e_a=(RH_{mean}/100)[e^\circ(T_{max})+e^\circ(T_{min})]/2. Wind conversion is u2=uz4.87/ln⁡(67.8z−5.42)u_2=u_z4.87/\ln(67.8z-5.42) with z = 10 m. These are FAO-56 equations 19 and 47. Mean RH is less preferable than paired humidity extremes when available. The available Tmin vapour-pressure fallback is not used to fill RH here.
Net radiation uses absorbed shortwave and FAO-estimated longwave radiation; the solar/clear-sky radiation ratio is capped at 1. Pressure and gamma depend on elevation. Solar geometry retains the FAO denominator 365 even in leap years; monthly sums include every actual date, including 29 February. Polar day/night is outside the implementation’s scope.
Monthly mean weather cannot exactly reproduce daily ET0 because the equation is nonlinear. Changing wind or humidity assumptions requires authorized daily inputs and recalculation, rather than the monthly tables.
Relation to Zomer et al. (2022)
The global database described by Zomer et al. also uses FAO Penman–Monteith reference evapotranspiration (Zomer et al. 2022). However, it uses WorldClim monthly climate data for 1970–2000, while this chapter uses daily NARO data for 2008–2018. The basic method is shared, but the inputs, time steps and resulting values are not identical.
Published FAO check
The Uccle example (6 July, FAO-56 example 18) uses the published actual vapour pressure, rather than the NARO mean-RH approximation. The expected result is about 3.9 mm/day. This checks implementation, not the accuracy of every cell.

example_et0 <- pipeline_p0_et0_fao56(
  mean_temperature = matrix(16.9),
  maximum_temperature = matrix(21.5),
  minimum_temperature = matrix(12.3),
  solar_radiation = matrix(22.07),
  actual_vapour_pressure = matrix(1.409),
  wind_2m = matrix(pipeline_p0_wind_at_2m(10 * 1000 / 3600, 10)),
  elevation = 100,
  latitude = 50.80,
  day_of_year = 187
)
stopifnot(abs(as.numeric(example_et0) - 3.9) < 0.08)
data.frame(et0_mm_day = as.numeric(example_et0))

  et0_mm_day
1   3.879455


Synthetic daily CSV
The CSV below contains three invented days for one cell. They do not constitute a July total. Matrices have one row per cell and one column per day. Latitude and elevation have one entry per row; day of year has one per column.

daily <- read.csv("data/examples/et0_daily_synthetic.csv")
as_row <- function(x) matrix(x, nrow = 1)
daily$et0_mm_day <- as.numeric(pipeline_p0_et0_fao56(
  mean_temperature = as_row(daily$mean_temperature_c),
  maximum_temperature = as_row(daily$maximum_temperature_c),
  minimum_temperature = as_row(daily$minimum_temperature_c),
  solar_radiation = as_row(daily$solar_radiation_mj_m2_day),
  actual_vapour_pressure = as_row(pipeline_p0_actual_vapour_pressure_rh(
    daily$relative_humidity_percent,
    daily$maximum_temperature_c,
    daily$minimum_temperature_c
  )),
  wind_2m = as_row(pipeline_p0_wind_at_2m(daily$wind_10m_m_s, 10)),
  elevation = daily$elevation_m[1],
  latitude = daily$latitude_degrees[1],
  day_of_year = as.integer(format(as.Date(daily$date), "%j"))
))
daily[c("date", "et0_mm_day")]

        date et0_mm_day
1 2008-07-05   3.513454
2 2008-07-06   3.784751
3 2008-07-07   4.002401


For gaps, call pipeline_p0_fill_short_gaps() separately on each year’s RH and wind before the equation, as in the local bundle’s export_yearly.R. The low-level pipeline_p0_monthly_sums() does not check calendar completeness: supply every date exactly once, in matching order, for a complete month (28/29/30/31 days) before reporting a monthly total.

title: Calculate FAO-56 Reference Evapotranspiration (ET₀)
text:
Local monthly products
Year-specific files contain 12 monthly totals per mesh/year, covering January 2008 through December 2018 (132 months per variable per cell). The means table contains 12 mean monthly totals: July is the mean of the eleven July totals. These are 11-year averages, not standard 30-year climate normals.
The prepared bundle covers 377,449 meshes, 153 primary-mesh blocks and 4,151,939 mesh-year rows. Its verification.csv records agreement of yearly averages with the supplied means within 1e-8 mm (maximum difference 4.77484718430787e-12 mm). This verifies aggregation, not meteorological accuracy. SHA256SUMS records bundle integrity.
Set PROJECT_DATA_DIR in the ignored .Renviron and restart R after editing. The following example is deliberately not executed during rendering:

bundle <- et0_data_dir() # PROJECT_DATA_DIR/naro-et0/2008-2018
normal <- read_monthly_csv(file.path(
  bundle,
  "data",
  "monthly_normals_2008_2018.csv.gz"
))
yearly_files <- list.files(
  file.path(bundle, "data", "yearly"),
  pattern = "^monthly_[0-9]{4}_2008_2018[.]csv[.]gz$",
  full.names = TRUE
)
# One block, not all Japan:
one_block <- read_monthly_csv(yearly_files[1])
period_summary(one_block, 7:9, "Jul-Sep")
winter_summary(one_block)

Base R reads gzip CSVs directly. read_monthly_csv() keeps mesh3_code as character. et0_data_dir() fails if the environment variable is unset. Monthly columns are et0_fao56_Jan through et0_fao56_Dec and precipitation_Jan through precipitation_Dec, in mm/month. See the bundle’s data-dictionary.csv and STATUS.md. Annual totals in the means table sum its 12 months. et0_filled_days is the maximum of separate RH and wind filled-day counts per cell/year, summed across 11 years in the means table. It is not their union or a count of missing days in all input variables.

title: Calculate FAO-56 Reference Evapotranspiration (ET₀)
text:
Month windows and AI
For July–September, add the three monthly ET₀ totals and the three precipitation totals:
ET0,7:9=∑m=79ET0,m=ET0,7+ET0,8+ET0,9,P7:9=∑m=79Pm=P7+P8+P9,AI7:9=P7:9ET0,7:9=P7+P8+P9ET0,7+ET0,8+ET0,9.
\begin{aligned}
ET_{0,7:9} &= \sum_{m=7}^{9} ET_{0,m} = ET_{0,7} + ET_{0,8} + ET_{0,9}, \\
P_{7:9} &= \sum_{m=7}^{9} P_m = P_7 + P_8 + P_9, \\
AI_{7:9} &= \frac{P_{7:9}}{ET_{0,7:9}}
         = \frac{P_7 + P_8 + P_9}{ET_{0,7} + ET_{0,8} + ET_{0,9}}.
\end{aligned}

Here, mm is the month number, ET0,mET_{0,m} and PmP_m are the monthly totals in mm, and 7:97:9 denotes July–September. AI is dimensionless. Do not multiply the monthly totals by days again. AI is sum(P)/sum(ET0) over identical months, rather than the mean of monthly AI. Missing months propagate and non-positive or missing ET0 denominators give NA. P−ET0 is a climatic water balance, not a soil-water balance model.
The synthetic CSV below has two invented identifiers and three years of illustrative monthly totals, independent of the daily example above.

yearly <- read_monthly_csv("data/examples/et0_monthly_synthetic.csv")
jas <- period_summary(yearly, 7:9, "Jul-Sep")
jas

  mesh3_code year  period et0_mm precipitation_mm aridity_index
1   00000001 2008 Jul-Sep     54              168     3.1111111
2   00000002 2008 Jul-Sep     69              198     2.8695652
3   00000001 2009 Jul-Sep    108              252     2.3333333
4   00000002 2009 Jul-Sep    123              282     2.2926829
5   00000001 2010 Jul-Sep    162               84     0.5185185
6   00000002 2010 Jul-Sep    177              114     0.6440678
  water_balance_mm
1              114
2              129
3              144
4              159
5              -78
6              -63

columns <- c(
  paste0("et0_fao56_", month.abb),
  paste0("precipitation_", month.abb)
)
normal <- yearly[yearly$year == 2008, "mesh3_code", drop = FALSE]
for (column in columns) {
  normal[[column]] <- vapply(
    normal$mesh3_code,
    function(key) {
      mean(yearly[yearly$mesh3_code == key, column]) # no na.rm
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
}
climate_jas <- period_summary(normal, 7:9, "Jul-Sep")
data.frame(
  mesh3_code = normal$mesh3_code,
  ratio_of_climatological_sums = climate_jas$aridity_index,
  mean_yearly_ai = vapply(
    normal$mesh3_code,
    function(key) {
      mean(jas$aridity_index[jas$mesh3_code == key])
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
)

         mesh3_code ratio_of_climatological_sums mean_yearly_ai
00000001   00000001                     1.555556       1.987654
00000002   00000002                     1.609756       1.935439


A ratio of climatological sums (the original production definition) generally differs from the mean yearly AI. Averaging monthly AI also changes the weighting:

p <- c(50, 200)
et0 <- c(100, 50)
data.frame(ratio_of_sums = sum(p) / sum(et0), mean_monthly_ai = mean(p / et0))

  ratio_of_sums mean_monthly_ai
1      1.666667            2.25


Winter crosses years
Winter Y combines December Y−1 with January-February Y. period_summary(data, c(12, 1, 2)) only selects months within the same row. Use winter_summary() on year-specific rows for a chronological winter. It aligns by mesh and year, preserves input rows, and labels winter by the year of January-February. Missing prior December yields NA.

winter_summary(yearly)

  mesh3_code year                 period et0_mm precipitation_mm aridity_index
1   00000001 2008 Dec(previous year)-Feb     NA               NA            NA
2   00000002 2008 Dec(previous year)-Feb     NA               NA            NA
3   00000001 2009 Dec(previous year)-Feb     68              193      2.838235
4   00000002 2009 Dec(previous year)-Feb     83              223      2.686747
5   00000001 2010 Dec(previous year)-Feb    113              139      1.230088
6   00000002 2010 Dec(previous year)-Feb    128              169      1.320312

1               NA
2               NA
3              125

For the complete real export, winters ending in 2009–2018 are available. Winter 2008 lacks December 2007; winter 2019 lacks January-February 2019 and has no anchor row. Summing December, January and February means describes an average seasonal window, not a specific winter or its variability.

title: Calculate FAO-56 Reference Evapotranspiration (ET₀)
text:
Reproduction and verification
R/pipeline_p0_et0.R is unchanged from the standalone bundle, originating at japanese-trees-sdms commit 1731a9e9fcaba87d718168e5eed0aeaed68b2acd. The gap helper is extracted unchanged from its R/pipeline_p0_naro.R. R/et0_support.R adds CSV reading, paths and seasonal summaries. No new package dependency is required. The export environment was R 4.5.3 and terra 1.8.86, as recorded in the bundle’s build-environment.csv. Optional regeneration from authorized NetCDFs uses terra and the local bundle scripts. Raw inputs remain immutable. This integration does not retrain an SDM.
Download the calculation functions, support functions, synthetic daily CSV and synthetic monthly CSV.
From the project root:
Rscript --vanilla tests/test_et0.R
Rscript tests/verify_et0_local.R
quarto render notebooks/calculate_ET0.qmd --profile en
quarto render notebooks/calculate_ET0.qmd --profile ja
The first script uses base R and synthetic inputs. The second reads all local yearly tables via PROJECT_DATA_DIR, validates keys and coverage, and compares their means with the supplied table. It prints aggregate statistics only. Rendering this chapter never reads NARO tables.

title: Calculate FAO-56 Reference Evapotranspiration (ET₀)
text:
References

Allen et al. (1998), Crop evapotranspiration, FAO Paper 56: equation and surface, inputs, worked examples.

NARO Agro-Meteorological Grid Square Data System, obtained using agrmesh (Murakami and Nagasaki, 2023).

NARO usage terms and application guide: apply for access yourself and check the conditions before using the data.

For further reading:


Global ET₀ and AI: Zomer et al. (2022) describe the global database introduced above (Zomer et al. 2022).

How NARO temperature and precipitation data are made: Ohno et al. (2016) explain how observations, numerical forecasts and climate normals are combined to produce daily 1 km grid data (大野 et al. 2016).

Snow modelling with NARO data: Kominami et al. (2015) describe a snow water equivalent model using grid weather data (小南 et al. 2015). This is background reading on NARO data applications; snow water equivalent is not an input to the ET₀ calculation in this chapter.







Zomer, Robert J., Jianchu Xu, and Antonio Trabucco. 2022. “Version 3 of the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database.” Scientific Data 9 (1): 409. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01493-1.


大野宏之, 佐々木華織, 大原源二, and 中園江. 2016. “実況値と数値予報，平年値を組み合わせたメッシュ気温・降水量データの作成.” 生物と気象 16: 71–79. https://doi.org/10.2480/cib.J-16-028.


小南靖弘, 広田知良, 井上聡, and 大野宏之. 2015. “メッシュ農業気象データのための積雪水量推定モデル.” 雪氷 77 (3): 233–46. https://doi.org/10.5331/seppyo.77.3_233.

title: Get Nearest Climate Value by Coordinates
text:
Load library
日本語はこちら（JP）
This chapter introduces get_nearest_climate_value(), which returns climate variable values from the nearest mesh cell to given coordinates. The function source file is R/get_nearest_climate_value.R.
library(sf)

title: Get Nearest Climate Value by Coordinates
text:
Load data

data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROJECT_DATA_DIR")
sf_climate <- readRDS(file.path(
  data_dir,
  "climate_mesh_data_joined/climate_mesh_data_with_aridity_index.rds"
))

title: Get Nearest Climate Value by Coordinates
text:
Define the function

source("R/get_nearest_climate_value.R")

title: Get Nearest Climate Value by Coordinates
text:
Usage
Get nearest aridity_index for one coordinate

result <- get_nearest_climate_value(
  sf_climate,
  lon = 139.6917,
  lat = 35.6895,
  value_col = "aridity_index"
)
print(result)

Get multiple variables for one coordinate

result <- get_nearest_climate_value(
  sf_climate,
  lon = 139.6917,
  lat = 35.6895,
  value_col = c("aridity_index", "precipitation_year")
)
print(result)

Get one variable for a data frame of coordinates

df_input <- data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  longitude = c(139.6917, 135.5022, 130.4181),
  latitude = c(35.6895, 34.6937, 33.5902)
)
result <- get_nearest_climate_value(
  sf_climate,
  df = df_input,
  lon_col = "longitude",
  lat_col = "latitude",
  value_col = "aridity_index"
)
print(result)

Get nearest values for a data frame of coordinates

df_input <- data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  longitude = c(139.6917, 135.5022, 130.4181),
  latitude = c(35.6895, 34.6937, 33.5902)
)
result <- get_nearest_climate_value(
  sf_climate,
  df = df_input,
  lon_col = "longitude",
  lat_col = "latitude",
  value_col = c("aridity_index", "precipitation_year")
)
print(result)

Get all attributes

result <- get_nearest_climate_value(
  sf_climate,
  lon = 139.6917,
  lat = 35.6895,
  value_col = NULL
)
print(head(result))

title: Appendix A — Plot Japan Climate Map
text:
Load data
日本語はこちら（JP）
This chapter draws Japan climate maps using tmap and rnaturalearth.
data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROJECT_DATA_DIR")
sf_climate <- readRDS(file.path(

title: Appendix A — Plot Japan Climate Map
text:
Plot PET

# renv::install("ropensci/rnaturalearthhires")
variable <- "PET_year"
japan <- ne_states(country = "Japan", returnclass = "sf")
sf_plot <- sf_climate[!is.na(sf_climate[[variable]]), ]
tm <- tm_shape(japan, crs = 4612) +
  tm_polygons(col = "gray90") +
  tm_shape(sf_plot[, variable], crs = 4612) +
  tm_fill(
    fill = variable,
    fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "viridis"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = variable,
      reverse = TRUE,
      position = c("right", "bottom"),
      frame = FALSE,
      bg.color = "transparent"
    )
  ) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, bg.color = "transparent")
print(tm)

output_dir <- "output"
dir.create(output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
tmap_save(
  tm,
  filename = file.path(
    output_dir,
    paste0("japan_climate_map_", variable, ".png")
  ),
  dpi = 300
)



PET map result; Data source: National Land Numerical Information Download Site, Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, Japan. URL: https://nlftp.mlit.go.jp/ksj/gml/datalist/KsjTmplt-G02-v3_0.html

Plot monthly Aridity Index
The same map can be drawn for each monthly AI column. Run the loop to save one PNG per month.

japan <- ne_states(country = "Japan", returnclass = "sf")
month_labels <- month.abb
for (month in seq_along(month_labels)) {
  month_label <- month_labels[month]
  variable <- paste0("aridity_index_", month_label)
  sf_plot <- sf_climate[!is.na(sf_climate[[variable]]), ]
  tm <- tm_shape(japan, crs = 4612) +
    tm_polygons(col = "gray90") +
    tm_shape(sf_plot[, variable], crs = 4612) +
    tm_fill(
      fill = variable,
      fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(
        values = "viridis"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = variable,
        reverse = TRUE,
        position = c("right", "bottom"),
        frame = FALSE,
        bg.color = "transparent"
      )
    ) +
    tm_layout(
      frame = FALSE,
      bg.color = "transparent"
    )
  print(tm)

  tmap_save(
    tm,
    filename = file.path(
      output_dir,
      paste0("japan_climate_map_", variable, ".png")
    ),
    dpi = 300
  )
}

title: Appendix B — One QMD, Two Languages: A Quarto Guide
text:
What you will build
日本語はこちら（JP）
Keep English prose, Japanese prose and shared R code in one source file per page. Build two sets of HTML, then link matching pages with JP/EN buttons. Editing the calculation once updates both language versions on the next build. Translations still need to be written and reviewed by a person.
This is the method used by this site and by leaf-mechanics-dehydration. The diagram separates building the site from reading the site.
When reading: the browser opens an already built page. It does not run R, render Quarto, or translate the page. Keep both language outputs available.

title: Appendix B — One QMD, Two Languages: A Quarto Guide
text: One shared QMD builds English and Japanese HTML; the reader follows JP/EN links between those pages.
crumbs: B  Build a Bilingual Quarto Site

title: Appendix B — One QMD, Two Languages: A Quarto Guide
text:
Try a small project first
The following is a complete minimal example for a new practice folder. It is not a replacement for this repository’s climate-analysis configuration. Install Quarto and, for the shared R example, R with knitr and rmarkdown. This repository already manages its R packages with renv; use its usual renv::restore() workflow instead of adding a second package setup.
Create this layout. docs/ will be generated; do not write translations there.
practice/
  _quarto.yml
  _quarto-en.yml
  _quarto-ja.yml
  index.qmd
  language-switch.html
  filters/
    language-title.lua
  docs/                       # generated / 自動生成
    index.html
    ja/
      index.html

Step 1: Put shared settings in _quarto.yml
A profile is a named set of build settings. The group below makes en and ja alternatives, with en as the default. The book chapters and formatting are shared. The Japanese profile will override the output directory.


_quarto.yml

profile:
  group:
    - [en, ja]

project:
  type: book
  execute-dir: project
  output-dir: docs

book:
  title: "My bilingual notebook"
  chapters:
    - index.qmd

filters:
  - filters/language-title.lua

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    include-after-body: language-switch.html



Step 2: Add the two language profiles
lang selects Quarto’s interface language, such as the table-of-contents label. It does not translate your prose. Use separate output directories so the Japanese build does not replace the English HTML.
The navbar links initially point to the home page. Step 5 will make them follow the matching page when more chapters are added.


_quarto-en.yml

lang: en

book:
  navbar:
    right:
      - text: "JP"
        href: ja/index.html



_quarto-ja.yml

lang: ja

project:
  output-dir: docs/ja

book:
  title: "私の日英ノート"
  navbar:
    right:
      - text: "EN"
        href: ../index.html



Step 3: Write both languages in index.qmd
unless-profile="ja" shows English when the Japanese profile is inactive; when-profile="ja" shows Japanese when it is active. :::: opens and closes a language block. Keep these delimiters on their own lines, with blank lines around them.
The executable R chunk is outside both language blocks. Both builds use the same calculation, mean(c(1, 2, 3)), whose result is 2. The #language-switch ID identifies the link used by the navbar script. Only one such link should remain in each rendered page.


index.qmd

---
title: "A small calculation"
title-ja: "小さな計算例"
---

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="ja"}

[日本語はこちら（JP）](ja/index.html){#language-switch hreflang="ja" lang="ja"}

## Mean of three numbers

We calculate the arithmetic mean of 1, 2 and 3.

::::

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="ja"}

[Read this page in English (EN)](../index.html){#language-switch hreflang="en" lang="en"}

## 3つの数の平均

1、2、3の算術平均を計算します。

::::

```{r}
#| label: shared-mean
mean(c(1, 2, 3))
```







ImportantVisibility and execution are different



Hiding a prose block is not an execution control. Do not put expensive or data-reading R chunks inside the language blocks to prevent them from running. Use chunk options such as eval: false to control execution explicitly. Shared source code may still execute once per language build; sharing the code does not guarantee that the computation runs only once in total.




Step 4: Select the translated page title with a small Lua filter
title-ja is our own metadata field. The filter below replaces title only when lang is ja; it also supports an optional subtitle-ja field. Lua is included with Quarto, so no additional R package is needed for this step.


filters/language-title.lua

function Meta(meta)
  if pandoc.utils.stringify(meta.lang) == "ja" then
    for _, field in ipairs({"title", "subtitle"}) do
      if meta[field .. "-ja"] then
        meta[field] = meta[field .. "-ja"]
      end
    end
  end
  return meta
end



Step 5: Make the navbar switch to the same page
The page-level links already work without JavaScript. This script copies that page’s language link into the navbar, so switching from the ET0 chapter opens the other ET0 chapter rather than returning to the home page.
Save it as language-switch.html, referenced by include-after-body in Step 1. Keep the navbar labels exactly JP and EN, as those are the labels the script looks for. A Japanese flag is optional: this site’s language-switch.css uses an embedded SVG, which avoids platform-dependent flag emoji rendering. To reuse that decoration, copy the CSS file and add css: language-switch.css under format: html: in the common configuration.


language-switch.html

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {
  const target = document.querySelector("#language-switch");
  if (!target) return;
  for (const link of document.querySelectorAll(".navbar-nav .nav-link")) {
    if (["JP", "EN"].includes(link.textContent.trim())) {
      link.href = target.href;
      link.hreflang = target.hreflang;
      link.setAttribute("aria-label", target.textContent.trim());
    }
  }
});
</script>



Step 6: Build both languages and check them in a browser
From the practice folder, run these commands in order. The small example has no automatic post-render hook, so both commands are required.
quarto render --profile en
quarto render --profile ja
quarto preview --profile en
Open the local address printed by quarto preview, then test the page link and navbar switch in both directions. Both pages should show the number 2, with their own title and explanatory text. If you edit the Japanese prose afterward, rebuild the Japanese profile before checking it again.
For a chapter under notebooks/, use these relative links. A link is resolved from the generated HTML’s directory, not from the repository home page. Here example is the name of your new chapter, not a page in this site.







Page being read
Link to the other language




English home: docs/index.html
ja/index.html


Japanese home: docs/ja/index.html
../index.html


English chapter: docs/notebooks/example.html
../ja/notebooks/example.html


Japanese chapter: docs/ja/notebooks/example.html
../../notebooks/example.html





Step 7: Use the existing automation in this repository
This site adds a convenience layer to the minimal example:

_quarto-en.yml runs scripts/render-japanese.R after the English render.
The script builds Japanese pages when their sources have changed and keeps the English navigation index intact during the second build.
It also preserves the six old *_ja.html URLs with redirects and writes .nojekyll for GitHub Pages. These migration steps are specific to this site.

Therefore, in this repository, a normal quarto render builds both languages. An explicit quarto render --profile ja builds Japanese only. Do not put the Japanese post-render hook into _quarto.yml or _quarto-ja.yml: that could trigger repeated rendering. The hook’s paths and list of legacy URLs need adjustment before copying it into a different project.
When adding a chapter here:

Create a single QMD with both prose blocks, shared code and both titles.
Add it to the appropriate chapter/appendix list in both profile files.
Add its filename to the pages list in tests/check_bilingual.cjs.
Run the build and link check below. Check the actual page switches in a browser.
Commit the source change and generated docs/ together before publishing.

quarto render
node tests/check_bilingual.cjs

title: Appendix B — One QMD, Two Languages: A Quarto Guide
text:
If something does not work







Symptom
Check




Both languages appear in the body
The content-visible attributes, profile name, closing colons and blank lines


Japanese prose appears under an English title
title-ja, the Lua filter path and lang: ja


JP/EN always returns to the home page
The page-level #language-switch link and loaded navbar script


The other language gives a 404
Both builds exist, relative paths are correct, and both output trees were published


The Japanese page is out of date
The Japanese profile was rebuilt after the edit


A hidden chunk still reads data
Visibility is separate from execution; explicitly set eval: false


Editing docs/*.html has no lasting effect
Edit the QMD/configuration instead, then render



For GitHub Pages, a successful push is not the same as a successful deployment. Check the deployment for the pushed commit, then open both public language URLs. Publish from a completed, verified build; do not publish a folder while it is being rendered. Climate-data sharing restrictions still apply independently of the language-switching mechanism.
